title: DevRel, Part 2: Materiality and timing - what you must say, and when
subtitle: How to recognise that an incident or change is material, how the deadline is counted, and why silence is a choice with consequences
whyItMatters: Most of the damage in incident disclosure does not come from saying something false, it comes from saying it late. Telling material from immaterial and counting the deadline correctly is the technical part of the DevRel job, and it is the part you cannot improvise on the spot.
openingQuestion: Which of the following is almost certainly material and must be reported to developers using your API?
openingOptions: Data from some accounts was read without authorisation via the API
Switching the internal email provider used by every employee in the company
Launching a new brand identity after six months of preparation
Hiring 50 more customer service staff for the southern region
explanation: The test for materiality is: would a developer integrating your product have to change what they are doing on learning this - rotate keys, audit data, pause a rollout, or consider switching provider. Account data read without authorisation certainly would, because it forces them to check their own customers' data immediately. The other three would not - they may matter internally but they do not change a single line of code on the user's side. Note that the test does not depend on whether the news is good or bad, nor on whether the team has a fix ready yet. Waiting until the fix is ready is the single most common way the deadline gets missed, and the reasoning sounds entirely sensible from the inside.

diagram.label: Would someone integrating have to change what they do?
Yes → material → the disclosure clock starts
Disclose within the deadline, without waiting for a fix

realWorldExample.company: Rules on notifying personal data breaches
realWorldExample.description: GDPR in Europe and Decree 13/2023 in Vietnam both set a 72-hour deadline for notifying a personal data breach. What teams most often miss is not the definition of a breach - that is written down - but the moment the counting starts: the clock runs from when the organisation became aware of the breach, not from when leadership finished meeting about it.

quiz.question: What is the test for materiality?
options: Whether someone integrating would have to change what they are doing
Whether the incident lasted more than 10 minutes
Whether leadership regards the matter as important
Whether the change appears in the release notes
quiz.explanation: A threshold on duration or on the number of affected accounts is a support tool, not the definition. A very small change can still be material if it breaks other people's code - changing a field in a response from a number to a string touches almost no data and breaks every client that parses it. Equally, leadership's own sense of importance is not the test: the question is always about the developer on the other side of the API.

quiz.question: When does the disclosure clock start running?
options: When the internal meeting ends
When the event arises, not when the meeting ends
When the legal team finishes reviewing the draft announcement
When the first fix has been deployed to production
quiz.explanation: This is where deadlines are missed most often, and always with a reason that sounds entirely sensible from the inside: wait until there is a fix so the announcement is complete. If the clock started when internal work finished, any team could postpone any bad news indefinitely simply by keeping the work open, which is precisely why it does not start there.

quiz.question: Does a change that benefits users, such as doubling the API rate limit, have to be announced?
options: Only if you want to use it to promote the product
No, the duty to disclose applies only to adverse changes
Yes, materiality does not distinguish good news from bad
Only if a large customer asks for written notice of it
quiz.explanation: A higher rate limit also makes people redesign their systems - dropping a queue here, a cache there - so it has to be announced too. The obligation attaches to the size of the effect, not to its sign. Teams that announce good changes loudly and bad ones quietly build exactly the reputation that pattern deserves, and developers notice the asymmetry quickly.

quiz.question: Support tickets and complaint posts spike unusually, and the team has announced nothing. What should DevRel do?
options: Give extra free quota to keep the people complaining the loudest
Post a reassuring notice saying the system is operating normally
Nothing, because operations has not reached any official conclusion yet
Check internally which incident or change is causing it, and be ready to answer publicly
quiz.explanation: An unusual signal from outside usually means an incident has already happened and users saw it before you did. The first task is to find out what it is, because if something is wrong then the duty to disclose arose before the complaints did, not after. Posting reassurance before you know is worse than saying nothing: if the incident turns out to be real, the team has now made a false statement on top of a late one.

quiz.question: Why is silence a choice with consequences?
options: Because an information vacuum always gets filled with guesswork and rumour
Because regulators will treat any period of silence as deliberate concealment
Because customers will cancel at once
Because the press has a right to a reply
quiz.explanation: Users do not wait. Saying nothing does not mean nothing gets said - it only means someone else says it for you, with worse data. A thread on a developer forum speculating about an outage will be read by more people than your eventual post-mortem, and the longer the gap, the more that thread becomes the version people remember.

practicePrompt.question: On Tuesday morning the team finds that last week's deploy made webhooks send duplicate events to every integrating customer. Leadership wants to wait until Friday, when a fix is ready, and announce both together. Right or wrong?
options: Wrong: the clock runs from when the event arose, not from when a fix exists
Right: announcing with the fix helps users react more calmly
Right: you only disclose after leadership has met and approved the text
Wrong: wait until month end and put it in the regular release notes
practicePrompt.explanation: Material means someone integrating has to change what they do, and duplicate webhooks certainly clear that bar: every duplicate event may be an order processed twice on their side. The clock starts when the team KNOWS, not when the team is ready - otherwise any bad news could be postponed indefinitely on the grounds that a fix is being prepared. Three days of silence also creates a second risk: in that window users discover it themselves, word spreads on forums, and every day they write another batch of duplicate data that a single de-duplication check on their side could have stopped. The fix can still be announced later, as an update.

keyTakeaways: Material = someone integrating has to change what they do. Good or bad news makes no difference.
The clock runs from when the event arises, not from when the meeting ends or a fix exists.
A spike in support tickets with no announcement is a sign of an incident - investigate at once.
Silence is not neutral: the vacuum gets filled with rumour.

summary.keyIdea: Material means someone integrating has to change what they do - regardless of whether the news is good or bad
summary.commonMistake: Counting the deadline from when the person responsible for disclosure was told, when the clock actually runs from when the event arose.
summary.action: Review your internal process: from the moment an incident happens to the moment the person responsible for disclosure knows, how many hours pass.

application.title: Measure your own organisation's internal delay
application.message: Pick three incidents announced this year, find when each actually began and when the announcement was posted. That gap is your organisation's late-disclosure risk, measured with data rather than a feeling.
application.secondary: Very little damage comes from saying something wrong; nearly all of it comes from saying it late.

sections.text: Very little of the damage in incident disclosure comes from saying something wrong. Nearly all of it comes from saying it late, and almost every time the internal reason sounds reasonable: wait to be sure, wait for a fix, wait until after the holiday.

The only question is: would a developer who is integrating have to change what they are doing on learning this. A threshold on incident duration or number of affected accounts is only a support tool - some changes are tiny in the numbers yet break other people's code, like changing a field in a response from a number to a string.

items: The clock runs from when the event arises, not from when the DevRel team is told.
You may not wait until there is a fix - the fix is the content of the next announcement, not a condition of the first.
You may not wait for a time when fewer people are online.
If you do not have enough information yet, announce what is certain and say clearly what is still being verified.

sections.label: When users speak up and the team has said nothing
sections.text: An unusual spike in support tickets and complaint posts usually means users saw the incident before you did. The first task is not to post reassurance but to check what is actually happening - because if something is wrong, the duty to disclose arose before they spoke up.

This is where most mistakes happen, and it is not an ethical failure but a counting one. The disclosure clock runs from when the event ARISES, not from when the developer relations team is told, and not from when leadership finishes meeting to decide what to say. A deploy breaks webhooks on Wednesday afternoon, the on-call team knows on Thursday, engineering leadership meets on Friday, the person responsible for disclosure hears about it the following Monday - four days of the deadline have gone before the person accountable knows there is anything to do. That is why the hard part of this work lives in internal process, not in drafting the announcement.

sections.label: You may not wait until the information is complete
sections.text: A material event whose consequences are not yet fully known must still be disclosed, together with exactly that: this has happened, the impact is being assessed, an update will follow when there is more. Waiting for an exact figure is the most common cause of late disclosure, and it sounds very responsible - which is exactly what makes it dangerous. Very little damage comes from saying something wrong; nearly all of it comes from saying it late.

left.label: When users speak up and the team has said nothing
left.text: An unusual spike in support tickets usually means the incident has happened and users saw it before you. The first task is not drafting a denial but checking internally whether the incident is real - because if it is, silence is extending a period in which users keep writing broken data into their own systems.

right.label: Why silence is also a statement
right.text: When the community is asking and the team says nothing, people fill the gap with the worst assumption. No comment is a legitimate choice, but it has a price - and the price rises with every day of silence.

lines: This job runs on two clocks: the disclosure deadline and the rumour mill.
The second clock always runs faster.
